How to Conduct Due Diligence on a New Business Partner

A practical, step-by-step checklist for verifying a company or partner using public records: entity status, filings, liens, lawsuits, bankruptcy, licenses, and sanctions lists.

Key takeaways

  • ✓Start with entity status, then check liens, lawsuits, bankruptcy, and licenses.
  • ✓Government exclusion and sanctions lists are free to search.
  • ✓Keep a dated log of every check and treat public records as a starting point.

In this guide

  2. Step 2: Match the Details
  3. Step 3: Look for Secured Debts and Liens
  4. Step 4: Search Court Records

Before you sign a contract, share money, or hand over customer data, it pays to confirm that a business is what it says it is. Public records can answer many basic questions for free: whether the company legally exists, whether it is in good standing, whether it owes secured debts, and whether it has a history of lawsuits or bankruptcy. This checklist walks through each step and what to look for.

Step 1: Confirm the Business Exists

Search the Secretary of State (or equivalent business filing office) in the state where the company was formed. Record the exact legal name, entity type, formation date, status, and registered agent. A status such as "active" or "good standing" is a good sign. "Inactive," "revoked," "dissolved," or "delinquent" means the company may not be allowed to do business and deserves questions. Also check whether it is registered in your own state if it operates there.

Step 2: Match the Details

Compare the name, address, and officer names in the filing to what the partner told you and what appears on their contract and invoices. Differences are not always a problem, since companies use trade names and move offices, but unexplained differences are worth clearing up. Ask for a signed IRS Form W-9 and a certificate of good standing if the deal is significant.

Step 3: Look for Secured Debts and Liens

UCC filings, searchable through the Secretary of State in most states, show lenders who have a claim on a company's assets. County and state records may also show tax liens and judgment liens. A heavily encumbered company may have little left to satisfy a new creditor.

Step 4: Search Court Records

Search the company and its principals in county or state civil court records where they operate, and in federal courts through PACER or CourtListener. Look at how many cases exist, what they are about, and how they ended. A few contract disputes are ordinary for an established business. A pattern of unpaid vendors or fraud claims is not.

Step 5: Check Bankruptcy

Bankruptcy filings are in the federal court system. Search the business and its owners in PACER's Case Locator. A past bankruptcy does not automatically disqualify anyone, but it tells you about financial risk and the chapter filed, as described in our guide to Chapter 7 and Chapter 13.

Step 6: Verify Licenses and Registrations

If the work requires a license, such as contracting, real estate, healthcare, or financial services, verify it with the state licensing board and check for disciplinary actions. Public companies and some private fundraisings file with the SEC, and its EDGAR database is free to search.

Step 7: Screen Government Exclusion and Sanctions Lists

If you do business with government contractors or international parties, check the federal System for Award Management (SAM.gov) exclusion records and the Treasury Department's OFAC sanctions list search. These are free official tools.

Warning Signs

  • The company was formed very recently but claims a long track record.
  • The business is not in good standing, or its registered agent has resigned.
  • Names, addresses, or officers differ across documents.
  • Multiple lawsuits from vendors, customers, or employees on similar claims.
  • The partner will not provide basic documents or pushes you to skip checks.

Limits and Good Practice

Ownership details are not always public, so ask directly who owns and controls the business. A registered agent address is not an office, and many legitimate companies use a commercial agent. Save screenshots or copies of everything you rely on with the date. If you intend to run credit or background reports on individual people, rules such as the Fair Credit Reporting Act may apply, and an attorney can advise you. For large deals, public searches are a starting point, not a replacement for legal and financial review.

A Simple Due Diligence Log

Keep a short record of each check so that you can show what you verified and when. Useful columns are the check performed, the source, the date, what you found, and any follow-up needed. For example: "Business status, State Secretary of State, active, formed 2019, agent confirmed." A log also makes it easier to repeat checks before renewing a contract.

Frequently Asked Questions

How long should this take? A basic check of entity status, liens, lawsuits, and bankruptcy for a small company can often be done in an hour or two, while a large or high-risk relationship needs more time and professional help.

What if I find a lawsuit? Read the case to see what it is about and how it ended. A single dismissed dispute is often not meaningful, while repeated claims of non-payment or fraud are more serious.

Should I tell the partner I am checking? Many businesses expect it and will provide documents. Being open about standard checks usually builds trust.

Is this enough? Public records show a company's legal and litigation history, not its current cash position or reputation. Combine them with references, financial statements, and contract protections.
